claims.text: The particles are initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Their premelting and melting behavior is governed by an interplay among chemical complexity, nanoscale phase-transition behavior, and varied particle configurations.
Increasing the number of constituent elements can affect whether nanoparticles form random, single-phase alloys.
Chemical complexity affects the thermal response of the Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Varied nanoparticle configurations affect the thermal response and produce unique premelting and melting behavior.
The relevant premelting and melting behavior can be directly observed in individual particles by in situ TEM or STEM.
The proposed comparison uses a single-metal nanoparticle, such as iron, as the baseline under the same conditions.
The Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will have a melting point 20% higher than the baseline single-metal nanoparticle.
The hypothesis applies to particles with diameters from 5 to 20 nm.
The hypothesis applies over a temperature range of 500–1000 °C.
The exact relationship among chemical complexity, phase-transition behavior, and particle configurations is not fully understood.
Melting point and phase-transition behavior are the measured outcomes in the proposed experiment.
A measured HEA melting point within 5% of the single-metal baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
